quotes_checked: 29 of 29 exact (every quote is a verbatim substring of the Berean verse; Ezek 36:26, Exod 8:15/9:12 and Acts 11:18 cited by reference only)

fixes.why: The phrase 'free will' is not a biblical term; it comes from later Christian and philosophical writing. The card never says so, so a reader may think the Bible itself poses the question in these words. Saying it is a statement of fact, not a verdict.
fixes.fix: Add after the first sentence: "The phrase 'free will' comes from later Christian and philosophical writing; the Bible's own words are about choosing, willing, drawing, hardening and being unwilling."

fixes.why: 'God's working in the will comes first' sets this reading apart as the one where God acts first, but the agreed block and reading 3 (grace that comes before any decision) say God acts first too. The label implies the other readings put human choice first.
fixes.fix: Change the end of the label to: "...: God's working changes the will so that it turns to him"

fixes.why: The summary lists compatibilism as a name Lutheran and Reformed readers use. It is a philosophers' label; many Lutherans decline it and leave the relation of God's work and human choice as a mystery the text does not resolve. Stating it for both traditions flattens a real difference.
fixes.fix: In the summary: "Lutheran and Reformed readers hold this under names of their own (the bondage of the will; and, among many Reformed readers and some Lutheran ones, compatibilism, the view that ... both true). Many Lutherans leave how God's working and a person's choosing fit together as a mystery the text does not explain." In the term note replace 'many Lutheran and Reformed readers' with 'many Reformed and some Lutheran readers'.

fixes.why: Readings 1 and 3 each answer the Pharaoh passage (Exod 9:12 with 8:15) but reading 2 is silent on it, though it is one of the most-cited texts on the question and this reading has its own account. The _why notes the gap.
fixes.fix: Add: "They read Exodus 9:12 with Exodus 4:21, where the LORD says he will harden Pharaoh's heart, and with Exodus 8:15, where Pharaoh hardens his own, as one event described from two sides."

fixes.why: Prov 21:1 and Prov 16:9 are both providence-over-plans verses, so reading 2 has two of its eight on the same point, while its strongest verse on God working in the hearer is absent from the card. Acts 16:14 is the text this reading cites first for the opening of a heart in response.
fixes.fix: Replace Proverbs 21:1 with Acts 16:14: quote "The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul's message." note "God opens the heart, and the response follows."

fixes.why: The Hebrew of Gen 4:7 is notoriously hard (who desires whom, and whether 'master' is command or promise) and translations differ. The note states the reading with no sign that the Berean is one of several renderings.
fixes.fix: Note: "Read as God telling Cain that mastery is his to exercise (the Hebrew is hard, and translations differ)."

fixes.why: 'Prevenient grace' is a Wesleyan term and the label is given in it. Anabaptist writers mostly speak of free decision and discipleship, not of prevenient grace, so placing them under that label overstates their fit. The summary half-says this but the label does not.
fixes.fix: Summary: "...and Anabaptist readers, who mostly speak in other terms, put weight on the call to a free, adult decision to follow Christ."

summary: All quotes are the Berean's exact words and no reading is ranked, but a label that implies only reading 2 puts God first, a missing answer on Pharaoh for reading 2, and unmarked Lutheran differences over compatibilism leave small tilts. With the seven wording and verse fixes, a scholar of religion and a literary teacher could both accept it.
